title: Chapter 119 — The Candles
paragraphs: It is the warmest climates that nurse the cruelest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of never-fading green. It is the most dazzling skies that carry the deadliest thunders in their basket: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner meets the most terrible of all storms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst out of that cloudless sky like a bomb exploding on a dazed and sleepy town.

Toward evening of that day, the Pequod had her canvas torn away and, bare-poled, was left to fight a typhoon which had struck her directly ahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the thunder and blazed with the lightning that showed the disabled masts fluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the storm had left for its after-sport.

Holding on to a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck, glancing aloft at every flash of lightning to see what further disaster might have befallen the intricate rigging there, while Stubb and Flask were directing the men in hoisting the boats higher and lashing them more firmly. But all their efforts seemed in vain. Though hoisted to the very top of the cranes, the windward quarter boat (Ahab's) did not escape. A great rolling sea, dashing high against the reeling ship's tall, teetering side, stove in the boat's bottom at the stern, and left it again, dripping through like a sieve.

"Bad work, bad work, Mr. Starbuck," said Stubb, looking at the wreck, "but the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can't fight it. You see, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps — all round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me, all the start I have to meet it is just across the deck here. But never mind; it's all in fun, so the old song says —" (Sings.)
Oh! jolly is the gale, / And a joker is the whale, / A-flourishing his tail — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
The scud all a-flying, / That's his flip only foaming; / When he stirs in the spicing — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
Thunder splits the ships, / But he only smacks his lips, / A-tasting of this flip — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
"Enough, Stubb," cried Starbuck, "let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if you are a brave man you will hold your peace."

"But I'm not a brave man; I never said I was a brave man; I'm a coward, and I sing to keep my spirits up. And I'll tell you how it is, Mr. Starbuck: the only way to stop my singing in this world is to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I'll sing you the doxology to wind up with."
"Madman! Look through my eyes if you have none of your own."
"What! How can you see better on a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"

"Here!" cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder and pointing his hand toward the weather bow. "Don't you see that the gale comes from the east, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? The very course he swung to at noon today? Now look at his boat there; where is it stove? In the stern-sheets, man, where he always stands — his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard and sing away, if you must!"
"I don't half understand you; what's in the wind?"

"Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," mused Starbuck suddenly, paying no attention to Stubb's question. "This gale that now hammers at us to stave us in — we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us toward home. Over there, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward — I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
Just then, in one of the spells of deep darkness that followed the flashes, a voice was heard beside him, and almost at the same moment a volley of thunderclaps rolled overhead.
"Who's there?"
"Old Thunder!" said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain by angled lances of fire.

Now, just as the lightning rod on a spire ashore is meant to carry the dangerous fluid off into the soil, so the similar rod that some ships at sea carry to each mast is meant to conduct it into the water. But this conductor must reach down to a considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and, moreover, if it were kept towing there all the time, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering more than a little with some of the rigging and more or less slowing the vessel's way through the water. Because of all this, the lower parts of a ship's lightning-rods are not always overboard; they are generally made in long slender links, so that they can more readily be hauled up into the chains (the ledges outside the hull where the shrouds are fastened), or thrown down into the sea, as occasion requires.

"The rods! The rods!" cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly warned to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been darting like torches to light Ahab to his post. "Are they overboard? Drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!"

"Stop!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we are the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himalayas and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but away with privileges! Let them be, sir."
"Look aloft!" cried Starbuck. "The corpusants! The corpusants!"

The tips of all the yardarms were lit with a pale fire — the corpusants, or St. Elmo's fire. Each of the three tall masts, touched at every three-pronged end of its lightning-rod with three tapering white flames, burned silently in that sulfurous air like three gigantic wax candles before an altar.

"Blast the boat! Let it go!" cried Stubb at this instant, as a washing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand as he was passing a lashing. "Blast it!" But slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone, he cried: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

To sailors, oaths are everyday words; they will swear in the trance of the calm and in the teeth of the tempest; they will hurl curses from the topsail-yard-arms when most they teeter over a seething sea; but in all my voyaging, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship — when His Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin — the writing on Belshazzar's wall — has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pale fire burned aloft, the spellbound crew said little. They stood in one thick cluster on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence like a distant constellation of stars. Outlined against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet-black negro, Daggoo, loomed up to three times his real height and seemed to be the black cloud the thunder had come from. Tashtego's parted lips showed his shark-white teeth, which gleamed strangely as if they too had been tipped with corpusants; and, lit up by the unnatural light, Queequeg's tattoos burned on his body like Satanic blue flames.

At last the whole scene faded along with the pale fire aloft, and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two went by; then Starbuck, going forward, bumped into someone. It was Stubb. "What do you think now, man? I heard your cry; it wasn't the same as in the song."

"No, no, it wasn't; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces? Have they no sympathy for a laugh? And look, Mr. Starbuck — but it's too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock-full of sperm-oil, d'you see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three sperm candles — that's the good promise we saw."

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into view. Glancing upward, he cried: "See! See!" And once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled otherworldliness in their pallor.
"The corpusants have mercy on us all," cried Stubb again.

At the foot of the mainmast, right under the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee knelt in front of Ahab, but with his head bowed away from him. Close by, a number of seamen who had just been securing a spar up in the arched, overhanging rigging were caught and held by the glare; they now huddled together and hung there like a cluster of numbed wasps from a drooping orchard twig. Others stood rooted to the deck in various spellbound poses, like the standing, stepping or running skeletons at Herculaneum; but every eye was turned upward.

"Aye, aye, men!" cried Ahab. "Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame only lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I want to feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it — blood against fire! So."

Then, turning — with the last link still gripped in his left hand — he set his foot on the Parsee, and with his eyes fixed upward and his right arm flung high, he stood upright before the towering three-pronged trinity of flames.

"Oh! You clear spirit of clear fire, whom I once worshipped on these seas as a Persian, until in the sacramental act I was so burned by you that to this hour I bear the scar — I know you now, you clear spirit, and I know now that the right way to worship you is defiance. You will be kind to neither love nor reverence; and even for hate you can only kill; and all are killed. It is no fearless fool who faces you now. I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life I will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though only a point at best — wherever I came from, wherever I go — yet while I live on earth, the queenly personality lives in me and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in your lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss you; but at your highest, come as mere supernal power, and though you launch navies of fully laden worlds, there is something in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, you clear spirit, you made me out of your fire, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to you."
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames shoot up lengthwise to three times their former height; Ahab, like the rest, shuts his eyes, pressing his right hand hard over them.]

"I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; didn't I say so? Nor was it wrung out of me; nor do I drop these links now. You can blind; but then I can grope. You can consume; but then I can be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; my eyeballs ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Blindfolded, I will still talk to you. Light though you are, you leap out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of you! The javelins stop; open, eyes; do you see, or not? There burn the flames! Oh, you magnanimous one! Now I do glory in my genealogy. But you are only my fiery father; my sweet mother I do not know. Oh, cruel! What have you done with her? There lies my puzzle; but yours is greater. You do not know how you came to be, and so you call yourself unbegotten; you certainly do not know your beginning, and so you call yourself unbegun. I know something of myself that you do not know of yourself, oh you omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond you, you clear spirit, to whom all your eternity is only time, all your creativeness mechanical. Through you, your flaming self, my scorched eyes dimly see it. Oh, you foundling fire, you hermit immemorial, you too have your incommunicable riddle, your unshared grief. Here again, with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! Leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with you; I burn with you; I long to be welded with you; defiantly I worship you!"
"The boat! The boat!" cried Starbuck, "look at your boat, old man!"

Ahab's harpoon, the one forged in Perth's fire, was still lashed firmly in its conspicuous crotch, so that it stuck out beyond the bow of his whaleboat. But the sea that had stove in the boat's bottom had knocked off the loose leather sheath, and from the sharp steel barb there now streamed a level flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent's tongue, Starbuck seized Ahab by the arm. "God, God is against you, old man; hold back! This is an evil voyage! Badly begun, badly continued. Let me square the yards while we still can, old man, and make a fair wind of it for home, and go on a better voyage than this."

Hearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew ran to the braces at once — though not a single sail was left aloft. For the moment they seemed to share all the horrified mate's thoughts, and they raised a half-mutinous shout. But Ahab flung the rattling lightning links down on the deck, snatched up the burning harpoon, and waved it among them like a torch, swearing he would run it through the first sailor who so much as cast loose a rope's end. Petrified by his look, and shrinking still more from the fiery dart in his hand, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab spoke again:

"Every oath you swore to hunt the White Whale binds you as tightly as mine binds me; and heart, soul and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And so that you may know what tune this heart beats to — look here: this is how I blow out the last fear!" And with a single blast of breath he put out the flame.

As in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men flee the neighborhood of some lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength only make it all the more unsafe, because all the more a target for thunderbolts; so at those last words of Ahab's, many of the sailors did run from him in a terror of dismay.
